title: IPv6 Router Advertisement Options for DNS Configuration
summary: Specifies IPv6 Router Advertisement options that let routers tell hosts the addresses of DNS recursive servers and a DNS search list. It is a proposed standard, obsoletes RFC 5006, and was itself replaced by RFC 8106.

plainLanguage.summary: When your computer joins a network, the router can hand it the address of the internet phone book and tips for looking names up.

questions: how do ipv6 hosts learn dns servers
what is the ipv6 rdnss option
how do ipv6 hosts get dns servers from router advertisements
subtitle: Two IPv6 Router Advertisement options that tell hosts which DNS servers and search domains to use.

tldr.problem: IPv6 stateless autoconfiguration gives a host an address and a router but no way to learn its DNS servers, and almost every host needs DNS. Manual setup is impractical for nomadic hosts.
tldr.mechanism: Routers add two options to Router Advertisements: RDNSS, a list of recursive DNS server addresses, and DNSSL, a list of DNS search domain names. Each has a lifetime.
tldr.outcome: A host can configure its address and its DNS information from one message without DHCPv6. RFC 6106 has since been obsoleted by RFC 8106.

today: RFC 6106 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5006, and it has itself been obsoleted by RFC 8106. Use RFC 8106 for the current definition of these options.

sections.title: Why DNS Needs to Ride in Router Advertisements
sections.content:
IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and stateless address autoconfiguration can give a host addresses, default routers and a few other parameters. Most Internet services are named by DNS, but nothing in this machinery tells the host which DNS servers to ask. The RFC argues that stateless autoconfiguration cannot stand alone in a practical network without some DNS configuration.

DHCPv6 can supply the information, but this document defines an alternative based on Router Advertisement (RA) options, useful where there is no DHCPv6 infrastructure or some hosts lack a DHCPv6 client. The need is more critical in IPv6-only networks than in dual-stack networks that still have an IPv4 DNS server.

This specification standardizes the RDNSS option from the earlier Experimental RFC 5006 and adds the new DNSSL option. The routers must get their DNS information by manual configuration or some other mechanism, which is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A new kid at school gets a map and a list of helpful teachers on the first day. The router hands a computer its list of 'name lookup' helpers the same way.

sections.title: The RDNSS and DNSSL Options
sections.content:
The Recursive DNS Server option uses ND option type 25. It holds one or more 128-bit IPv6 addresses of recursive DNS servers that all share one Lifetime. Length is in units of 8 octets, with a minimum of 3 for one address and 2 more for each additional address.

The DNS Search List option uses type 31. It holds one or more domain name suffixes, encoded as in RFC 1035 but never compressed, and padded with zeros to a multiple of 8 octets. Its minimum length is 2.

Lifetime is a 32-bit count of seconds. It SHOULD be between MaxRtrAdvInterval and 2*MaxRtrAdvInterval, all one bits means infinity, and zero means the entry MUST no longer be used. An address or name is only used while both the router lifetime and the option lifetime are still valid.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note lists some helpers and says how long the list is good for. A note with zero means 'forget those helpers'.

sections.title: How Hosts Process the Options
sections.content:
A host first checks that Length meets the minimum (3 for RDNSS, 2 for DNSSL). If valid, it SHOULD copy the values into its DNS Repository and the resolver configuration in order, otherwise it MUST discard the option. Entries already known only get a refreshed expiry, and a Lifetime of zero deletes them.

Hosts keep a limited number of entries, where three is recommended. When the list is full, the new entry replaces the one that will expire first. The first address in an option is preferred for lookups.

When information comes from several sources, a host MUST extract DNS information from RAs unless the user has set static DNS configuration. Information from DHCP takes precedence over RA information. Among RAs, those protected by Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) MUST be preferred over those that are not. Conflicting data from different sources or different interfaces can lead to problems, so administrators need to keep them consistent.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer keeps a short list of helpers, around three. New helpers push out the one whose time is nearly up, and helpers from a trusted source go first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker can send a Router Advertisement with a fraudulent RDNSS address, steering hosts to an unintended DNS server. A bogus DNSSL can make a host resolve an unqualified name to a different machine. The RFC views these as similar to existing Neighbor Discovery attacks, and says learning bad DNS information is no worse than learning bad router information.

The RFC recommends that Neighbor Discovery use SEND so the options are covered by signatures. It also notes that SEND cannot tell which valid routers are authorized to send the DNS options. It recommends that network devices block rogue RA messages containing these options from unauthorized nodes, as switches already do for rogue DHCPv6 servers.
sections.plainLanguage: A prankster could hand out a fake phone book. Signed notes and guards on the network ports help keep fake ones out.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 5006
sections.content: Compared with RFC 5006, this document adds the DNSSL option and clarifies how RA and DHCP options coexist. It also clarifies the host procedure, sets a sufficient number of three for RDNSS addresses or search domains, and describes how to deal with several sources. It rewrites the implementation notes and the security considerations to cover more attacks and possible solutions, and it asks IANA for another ND option type for DNSSL.
sections.plainLanguage: The first version only listed phone book helpers. This version also adds hints for filling in half-typed names.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: In units of 8 octets; minimum 3 for one address.

fields.name: Lifetime
fields.desc: Seconds the addresses may be used; all ones means infinity.
